references.text: The men of Sodom were wicked and sinned greatly against the Lord, which provides the background for the great outcry and heavy sin mentioned in Genesis 18:20.
The Lord says He will go down to see if they have acted in accordance with the outcry that has reached Him – a direct continuation of 18:20.
The angels tell Lot that the outcry over Sodom has become so great before the Lord that He has sent them to destroy the city, a direct fulfillment of what is described in 18:20.
The Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah with sulfur and fire from heaven, as the final consequence of the great sin and outcry mentioned in 18:20.
Abel's blood cries out to God from the ground – a parallel to the outcry from Sodom and Gomorrah that reaches up to the Lord.
Ezekiel describes Sodom's sins in detail: pride, abundance of food, careless ease, and they did not help the poor and needy – an elaboration on the sin mentioned in Genesis 18:20.
God judged Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction and made them an example for the ungodly, showing the consequence of the serious sin mentioned in Genesis 18:20.

Sodom, Gomorrah, and the cities around them are an example of those who suffer the punishment of eternal fire because they indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh – a confirmation of the seriousness of the sin mentioned in Genesis 18:20.
Both verses describe a nation that incurs heavy guilt through gross offenses, which triggers God's judgment.
Both verses use the expression 'exceedingly great' to describe a state of total moral decay that demands God's judgment.
Both verses link an accumulated amount of sins directly to God's judgment and punishment.
Both verses identify specific actions so gross that they automatically trigger God's judgment.
The psalm describes the consequence (destruction) of the 'heavy sin' that is the theme of Genesis 18.
Romans provides the theological explanation for God's wrath as a reaction to the 'heavy sin' described in Genesis.
